models.summary: A carbon account for the living forest, then a stock predictor. Next year storage is this year plus growth, minus natural loss, minus the cut, from an initial store. The FAO series of stock, expansion, cut, and loss runs from 1990 to 2020. Storage is converted from volume by the IPCC defaults: understory 0.195, woodland 1.244, expansion 1.9, volume factor 0.5, carbon content 0.5, which the paper collapses to 1.158 times the volume. The printed substitution writes the woodland factor as 0.1.244. A forced regression has an R squared of 0.602 but variance inflation in the tens of thousands, so stepwise regression drops every driver but the lagged store, leaving next year equal to 0.999 times this year, with R squared 0.566 and F of 36.587. Stock itself is predicted by a back-propagation network on temperature, radiation, humidity, rain, age, and soil type, trained from nine stations, scaled into the unit interval, for 1000 passes toward an error of 0.000001 at a learning rate of 0.05. The fit correlates 0.95833 and the confirmation mean square error is 0.0508.
models.computational_cost: One stepwise regression on the FAO series and one network of 1000 passes

models.summary: Carbon held by wood products over their life, by three official methods. Storage is volume times density times the carbon rate. The stock-change approach counts products consumed inside the country, the production approach counts products of the growing country, and the atmospheric-flow approach counts the flow between the forest, the products, and the air. The three would agree if a country neither imported nor exported. On the global FAO series from 1990 to 2020 they differ, and no rule names a winner, so the paper takes the average. Product carbon is about one-fifth of living-forest carbon, and a product holds its carbon for nearly its whole life, which is the paper's reason to prefer some cutting over a ban.
models.computational_cost: One average of three accounting methods over 1990 to 2020

models.summary: A harvest plan over sub-compartments with four goals. A logged regression of service value keeps water, soil, and carbon, because their weights exceed 0.1, and drops nutrient accumulation, air purification, biodiversity, and recreation. Timber is added as the economic goal. Water regulation is ten times area times precipitation minus evaporation minus fast runoff, times a correction. Soil kept is area times the gap between the bare-land erosion and the forest erosion, times a correction. Each goal is scaled by its own minimum and maximum. The weights from the regression and the analytic hierarchy are 0.123 for carbon, 0.116 for water, 0.173 for soil, and 0.588 for timber. The cut is binary. A year cut cannot exceed that year growth, and it must stay within a band of the neighboring years. The slope caps a clear cut at 20, 10, or 5 hectares, land that already erodes is not cleared, and a stand must pass a minimum age and a minimum diameter. The timber weight is read as a reason to reject a ban.

models.summary: A century forecast and a five-stage plan for Jindong Forest in Yongzhou, Hunan: 635 square kilometers, 2.68 million cubic meters, mean slope 34 degrees, rain 1600 to 1900 millimeters, evaporation about 1225. The world model is kept for short forecasts and rebuilt here. Carbon density is stock per hectare times wood density times the biomass expansion times one plus the root ratio, times the carbon content. The forest keeps its share of the provincial area, planting finishes in 2050 and is spread evenly, and age classes step forward every five years. A logistic of age on stock fits with an R squared above 0.95. By 2120 the store is 450.003 teragrams at 102.55 megagrams per hectare, up from 240.727 in 2020. LINGO plans 425 sub-compartments in five stages of twenty years, with rain set at 1800 millimeters, bare-land erosion at 319.8, and yield at 0.65. The century cut is 9343.32 square meters and 2580341.86 cubic meters. The four increments are 289050.32 tonnes of carbon, 173476.02 of water, 9511.92 of soil, and 1677707.14 cubic meters of timber. If the best cycle is ten years longer than the present one, selective intensity stays under 40 percent and the wait is shortened until the best cycle is reached.
